p: This critical funding would enable us to sustain and expand crucial anti-hate, -bias, and -bigotry educational workshops for up to 14,000 students, deepen partnerships with NYC public schools and community groups, and respond quickly to emerging community tensions in real-time, such as the incident response and support we’ve provided to students and staff at JHS 194 William Carr, Hillcrest High School, and PS 261.

At a time when manifestations of hate are increasingly visible across various facets of society, particularly online, it is imperative that students receive direct instruction on investigating the harmful effects of fear-driven hate. Teachers are eager to address online hate, bullying, and bias but often lack the time, resources, and curriculum to navigate these complex topics. Such programming needs to be a high priority in New York City as NYPD hate crime statistics confirm an alarming escalation in hate incidents and hate crimes. During 2025, the NYPD Dashboard confirms 545 bias incidents, leading to 211 arrests, including 310 anti-Semitic (77 arrests), 59 anti-LGBTQIA+ (29 arrests), 43 anti-Black (16 arrests), 22 anti-Asian (14 arrests), 24 anti-Muslim (13 arrests) and 9 anti-Hispanic (7 arrests). In January 2026 alone, antisemitic incidents rose 182% from last year, with 31 hate crimes reported (20 more than in January 2025).

This program fosters a safe, inclusive learning environment, ensuring that difficult conversations are handled with sensitivity, respect for civil liberties, and a focus on youth leadership and allyship. Designed with a whole community approach, the workshop strengthens collaboration between students and the community. It creates a space for critical conversations about online safety and combating hate while also empowering youth to take an active role in creating solutions. As hate speech and bias-related incidents rise, programs like this are essential to fostering understanding and resilience in school communities.

We are also requesting your advocacy for a new $500,000 initiative proposal and support through Citywide Initiatives for Witness to History: Introduction to Testimony, a workshop for students in grades 9–12 that uses survivor testimony from the Holocaust and the Genocide Against the Tutsi in Rwanda to teach how history is created, remembered, and communicated. Witness to History addresses a gap not filled by existing school curricula: the cultivation of empathy grounded in media literacy by witnessing real human voices and a responsibility to respond to injustice in the present.

New York City stands at a pivotal educational moment: rising hate incidents, the fading presence of survivor testimony, and increasing historical misinformation converge to create an urgent need for media literacy. Witness to History offers a proven, research-informed response—one that does not merely teach about the past but shapes the citizens of New York’s future depends upon. Support at the requested level will ensure that thousands of young New Yorkers encounter history not as distant tragedy, but as living responsibility—carried forward through memory, empathy, and dialogue.

Witness to History addresses a gap not filled by existing school curricula: the cultivation of empathy grounded in media literacy by witnessing real human voices and a responsibility to respond to injustices from the Holocaust and Rwandan Genocide in the present. Research in

genocide and human-rights education demonstrates that testimony-based learning—encountering individual stories of survival, loss, and moral courage—is among the most powerful tools for reducing dehumanization and fostering long- term ethical awareness.

In communities that have experienced hate-based incidents or division—including schools navigating identity-based conflict—testimony-centered dialogue has proven to support healing, reflection, and renewed community trust. By moving students from passive observers of history to active moral participants, Witness to History strengthens the social fabric of New York City schools and prepares young people to confront hate, distortion, and indifference in their own generation.

We are grateful for your leadership and respectfully ask for your support of these requests. We look forward to continuing to partner with the City Council to deliver these vital services for New York City’s students and educators.

Thank you.

Good morning. Microphone check on Committee of Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. Today's date, March 10, 2026. Location, HR 1. Recorded by Kimberley Smith-Thomas.

Good morning, and welcome to today's New York City Council vote on the Committee of Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. At this time, please silence all electronic devices. Chair, you may begin.

[GAVEL] Thank you very much. I am Gale Brewer, Chair of the Committee of Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. Thank you for being here. I'd like to thank Council Members Stevens, Dinowitz, Morano, Zhuang, and Feliz for being here. We're voting on two bills. The first is my bill, Proposed Intro. 87-A. It combines the Archival Review Board and the Archives Reference and Research Advisory Board into a Library and Archival Review Advisory Board with nine members. The second is Deputy Speaker Williams' bill, Proposed Intro.

COMMITTEE ON GOVERNMENTAL OPERATIONS, STATE AND FEDERAL LEGISLATION 3 502-B, establishing a commission to review the salaries of elected officials in New York City and make recommendations regarding those salaries. The purviews of the Archival Review Board and the Archives Reference and Research Advisory Board are largely overlapping. That's why we're doing the Intro. They've been holding joint meetings since '23, and the most recent annual report, which came out January of this year, was also issued jointly. Combining the two Boards would not constitute a major change. Consolidation will save staff time and would increase efficiency while continuing to provide the agency with the same guidance and oversight the two separate boards offer. Members of the Boards are supportive of this change. The combination has been a topic raised by the Boards on many occasions, and members have repeatedly crafted proposals to consolidate the two Boards into one. I just want to point out what they look at, of the New York City Municipal Archives that have 200 million records, photographs, maps, government documents, and they are, in my book, very important. 502-B would establish a commission to review elected official pay. Elected official pay is

COMMITTEE ON GOVERNMENTAL OPERATIONS, STATE AND FEDERAL LEGISLATION 4 set by local law, but under our City's Administrative Code, the Mayor is required to appoint a commission to review the compensation levels of elected officials every four years and make recommendations to the Council. With the exception of the District Attorneys, the last time City elected officials received a raise was back in 2016. Mayor de Blasio failed to impanel the required commission in 2002. Mayor Adams also declined to convene one in 2024. The 10-year gap is the longest the City officials have gone without a raise in the 40 years the quadrennial commission framework has been in place. Over that time, salaries of New York elected officials have failed to keep pace with inflation and with the salaries of elected officials across the country. Legislators in Los Angeles, Chicago, and Philadelphia all make more than we do in New York, and all those cities have much smaller budgets and smaller workforces. Stagnant wages not only affect elected officials, while as we saw under Mayor Adams, some top executives can receive salaries that are significantly higher than the elected officials they serve. For most non-executive roles, the elected official salary serves as a cap on the salaries of

COMMITTEE ON GOVERNMENTAL OPERATIONS, STATE AND FEDERAL LEGISLATION 5 the employees who work under them. These salary caps can keep the City from offering competitive wages, which can keep us from being able to recruit the most talented individual for jobs. Low salaries can also negatively influence who is able to run for office. Being an elected official in New York is a challenging, demanding 24/7 job, as we all know, and officials should be able to support themselves and their families on their government salaries without needing to have a personal fortune. If salaries are too low, then elected officials' offices risk being accessible only to wealthy individuals. 502-B, which we'll be voting on today, requires the Mayor to convene a three-person commission to review the compensation levels of the Mayor, Public Advocate, Comptroller, Borough Presidents, Council Members, and DAs. The commission would have 75 days to make recommendations on new compensation levels. The commission would send their recommendations to both the Mayor and the Council. The Mayor would be able to send the Council approval, disapproval, or modifications of the commission's recommendations. The Council would then have discretion to review the recommendations and alter the compensation level of

COMMITTEE ON GOVERNMENTAL OPERATIONS, STATE AND FEDERAL LEGISLATION 6 the City's elected official. The bill would also require the calling of a commission every four years on '26. This will be in lieu of, and not in addition to, the commissions that are currently required to meet in 2028 and every four years after that. I would like to thank the following Council Staff for their work, from Government Ops Committee Staff, Johari Frasier, Erica Cohen, and Saiyemul Hamid, and from my Staff, Cynthia Hornig and Shula Puder, and everyone else. I will now turn it over to the Clerk to call the roll.
Thank you. William Martin, Committee Clerk. Roll call vote, Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. Items are coupled. Chair Brewer.

Aye.

Thank you very much. This hearing concludes. [GAVEL]
